text:
Midday in Burlington and the day is playing out the way the forecasters expected: cloudy and chilly, with temperatures already in the low 40s, about where the afternoon high of 43 will land. The system that brought yesterday's showers has moved off, so any leftover sprinkle should wrap up by 3 and add up to almost nothing. I wouldn't cancel anything over it, but a light jacket is smart, and with the sun setting around 4:25, a walk is best done early.

Tonight stays cloudy and cools to around 32, so a little frost on the windshield is possible in the morning. Monday looks much the same, mostly cloudy with a high near 44. The clouds are stuck under a lid of air that's slow to lift, so don't expect much sun until later in the day.

The better news is Tuesday. A big area of high pressure settles in, and it should feel more like mid-October, with highs near 50 and the 50s sticking around through the week. Tomorrow is a grab-a-jacket day, and the nice stretch starts after that.

AFD KEY MESSAGES (forecaster's reasoning, issued 2026-11-15T11:20:00+00:00 — covers the whole BTV area, northern NY included: translate to what Burlington feels, never repeat other regions' place names):
  1. Lingering upslope snow showers gradually taper off today.
  2. A warm, dry and mostly sunny week is in store.
AFD WHAT CHANGED (same regional caveat): As of 206 AM EST Sunday... No significant changes.
AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: The moist cyclonic flow will continue through tonight, but the shortwave responsible for the widespread showers yesterday has passed to the south, ending most of the synoptic forcing. A subsidence inversion will form today and begin to lower, keeping the clouds trapped under it, but also decreasing the moisture depth. By tonight, the moisture depth should be too shallow to produce precipitation. Overall, only a couple tenths of an inch of additional snow accumulations are expected today. Tonight into Monday, the lowering inversion should drop below summit height and cause undercast to develop. KEY MESSAGE 2: A potent ridge and associated area of surface high pressure will dominate the weather this week, making it feel as if it were still mid-October. In a classic El Nino pattern, deep troughing and strong surface lows over the Pacific have caused continuous southwest to westerly flow out west, flooding the Great Plains and western Canada with warm Pacific air. This has caused temperature anomalies in the 20-30+ degree range. This airmass will begin to arrive Monday, but clouds will likely remain stuck under the inversion, so it will likely take until Tuesday to warm up. From then through the end of the week, and now likely through the weekend, highs in the 50s will prevail, though 60 will be possible in some of the warmest areas. There will be a strong, persistent subsidence inversion, and it will aided by the fact that significantly more surface heat will be lost at night than will be able to be replenished by the sun during the day. Radiational cooling will help lows drop into the 20s and 30s, around climatological normals. Weak troughs will gradually erode the ridge from the north, but it looks like it will take through next weekend for the ridge to get pushed to the south and east. Therefore, cooler conditions and chances for precipitation to return will likely not occur until the start of the following week.

WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Mt. Mansfield received around 4 inches of snow on Saturday, marking the latest date to receive an inch of snow or greater. This breaks the previous record of November 9th, 1985. A general 1 to 4 inches of snow fell in the region, mainly in the mountains. This system responsible for this is moving out, so only scattered valley sprinkles and mountain flurries are expected, mainly this morning. It will remain mostly cloudy and a bit blustery through the afternoon with highs in the upper 30s to low 40s. The week will have a return to an extended period of dry and mild weather, similar to what we’ve had in October. Monday will be partly sunny with highs in the 40s. Tuesday through Thursday will have plenty of sunshine with highs mainly in the 50s. Some upper 50s are possible by Thursday, so any snow will melt through the week. A weak cold front may touch off an isolated shower on Friday, otherwise there’s the possibility for the dry stretch to continue into next weekend.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-15T13:59:00Z — same caveat): Drier Sunday, but staying chilly with lots of clouds — Sunday stays mostly cloudy and chilly, with highs in the low 40s. Expect a few lingering mixed showers in the morning, followed by a mostly dry afternoon. Southern Vermont can expect more breaks of sun. Tonight will be mostly cloudy and seasonably cold, with lows in the 20s and 30s. Clouds will be stubborn on Monday, though many towns should see a gradual clearing trend through the afternoon. Highs again reach the low 40s. Tuesday marks the transition toward brighter and warmer weather. Expect a partly to mostly sunny sky, with highs near 50. The Wednesday through Friday stretch looks beautiful, with partly sunny skies and highs reaching the mid to upper 50s. The mild and quiet pattern continues next weekend. Highs reach well into the 50s, with plenty of sun. A cooler, more seasonable airmass likely returns Thanksgiving week as highs fall back to the 40s. A few rain and snow showers are possible as a front passes through.
